title: Lark: Biologically Inspired Neuroevolution for Multi-Stakeholder LLM Agents

mechanism.domainTask: Multi-stakeholder strategy generation and decision support with LLM agents
mechanism.populationDetail: A size-k population of strategies evolves generation by generation; the paper does not describe persistent islands or a tree-structured search population.
mechanism.archiveDetail: No distinct historical elite archive is described; high-quality strategies survive through top-k selection into the next population.
mechanism.replacementDetail: The next generation is selected as the top-k from the previous population combined with matured duplicates; best solutions persist through survivor selection rather than a separate archive.
mechanism.generationDetail: The system initializes strategies from scratch, applies unary plasticity edits that preserve the core structure, and duplicates then specializes strong strategies for stakeholder subgroups.
mechanism.feedbackDetail: Structured feedback includes stakeholder ranks/Borda scores, token counts, penalized fitness, and population efficiency; no evaluator-generated natural-language critique is reused in prompts.
mechanism.parentSelectionDetail: The duplication probability is a sigmoid of score relative to population mean, and plasticity is unary; exact parent count is stage-dependent, with zero-parent initial sampling.
mechanism.outOfTaxonomy: Influence-weighted social-choice aggregation over heterogeneous stakeholder preferences is combined with a token-efficiency penalty; this multi-stakeholder objective construction is more specific than the current generic preference label.

provenance.sourcePdf: papers/Lark Biologically Inspired Neuroevolution for Multi-Stakeholder LLM Agents.pdf
provenance.citationWarning: Current survey citations under score-based parent selection and preference/ranking evaluation are supported. Make clear that Lark uses ordinal stakeholder ranks and Borda aggregation plus token penalty; fitness-relative duplication is sigmoid-based. Independent judges support repeated, not necessarily parallel, evaluation.
